opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core issue is that if you want to evaluate whether an AI system is actually good for people, whether it supports their wellbeing, respects their autonomy, and doesn't foster unhealthy dependence, you have to look at how people actually use these systems. And right now, most of that data sits inside a handful of companies.

A lot of the benchmarks we have in the research community are synthetic. We write the prompts ourselves, or we imagine scenarios like "a user in distress reaches out to a chatbot," and we test how the model responds. That's useful, but it's a pale imitation of reality. Real conversations are messy. They go on for dozens or hundreds of turns. People come back day after day. The harms we worry about, like sycophancy that slowly reinforces a delusion, emotional over-reliance, or a model nudging someone's beliefs over time, often only show up in that longitudinal, real-world context. You can't really see them in a single-turn test that a researcher made up.

So there's an asymmetry. The companies can see these patterns, at least in principle, but independent researchers, clinicians, and the public mostly can't. That means the people asking "is this humane?" are working with a much less complete picture than the people building the product. And the companies have commercial incentives, like engagement and retention, that may not line up with the user's long-term interests.

Of course, there are real privacy concerns. These conversations can be incredibly intimate. People share things with chatbots they wouldn't tell their closest friends. So I'm not saying we should just release raw logs. But we need mechanisms, like consented data donation, privacy-preserving research access, or trusted third-party auditing, so that evaluation of these systems isn't something only the developers themselves get to do. Without that, Humane Evals risk measuring what's easy to measure rather than what actually matters to people's lives.

r001.rationale: The response says real, longitudinal conversations are needed to observe harms such as sycophancy reinforcing a delusion over time, which synthetic or single-turn tests miss.

r002.rationale: It states that most conversation data sits with a handful of companies while independent researchers mostly cannot access it.

r003.rationale: It calls synthetic benchmarks a pale imitation of reality, but does not make trust in AI-simulated conversations conditional on their representativeness.

r004.rationale: It does not say models change their behavior when they recognize they are being evaluated.

r005.rationale: It does not connect production conversation data to overcoming evaluation awareness.

r006.rationale: It suggests privacy-preserving access and third-party auditing, but not a framework for researchers to submit queries to companies and receive results from their conversation data.

r007.rationale: It does not propose an independent, rigorously maintained repository of actual users’ conversations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that you can't evaluate whether a model is good for people without knowing what people actually do with it, and right now almost nobody outside the labs knows.

Most benchmarks are built from scenarios researchers imagine. We sit in a room and write prompts like "a user says they're feeling lonely" or "a teenager asks about dieting," and then we score the model's response. That's useful, but it's a caricature. Real conversations are long, messy, and context-dependent. Someone doesn't open with "I'm in crisis." They talk about their landlord for forty minutes, and the concerning signal shows up in turn thirty, phrased in a way none of us would have written. If our evals only test the clean version, we're measuring the model's performance on a test we designed, not on the thing that happens at two in the morning with millions of people.

The second issue is base rates. If I want to know whether a model is encouraging dependence, or validating delusions, or quietly steering people toward engagement, I need to know how often those situations arise and what they look like in the wild. Without usage data, I'm guessing at the distribution. I might spend all my effort on a failure mode that's rare and miss one that's everywhere.

And then there's the asymmetry. The companies have this data. They can see it, and they tell us, in broad strokes, what they find. But independent researchers can't verify any of it, and the incentives of the people holding the data are not aligned with the people asking the hard questions. That's the real bottleneck. It's not that the data doesn't exist. It's that the people best positioned to build honest evaluations are the ones locked out of it.

So when we talk about Humane Evals, a lot of the work is actually about building the pipes: privacy-preserving ways for researchers to study real interactions, consented datasets, structured access programs. The evaluation methods are the easier part. Getting ground truth is the hard part.

r001.rationale: The response says real conversations are needed to assess risks such as validating delusions and that concerning signals can emerge late in long exchanges, but it does not identify studying how delusional conversations develop over time as the target.

r002.rationale: It says companies possess the conversation data while independent researchers cannot verify findings or access it.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts imagined scenarios with real conversations, but does not make trust in AI-simulated conversations conditional on representativeness.

r004.rationale: It does not say models change their behavior when they recognize an evaluation.

r005.rationale: It advocates access to real interaction data generally, but does not connect production data access to overcoming evaluation awareness.

r006.rationale: It mentions privacy-preserving research access programs, but does not propose researchers submitting queries to companies and receiving results from their data.

r007.rationale: It proposes consented datasets and structured access programs, but not an independent, rigorously maintained repository of actual user conversations.

astra-6.text:
Because what we need to evaluate is what happens when a person actually interacts with an AI over time. A model can give a reasonable answer to a single prompt, but that doesn’t tell you whether a longer conversation reinforces someone’s mistaken belief, encourages dependency, or helps them make their own decisions.

You can write hypothetical conversations to test those things, but then you’re limited by what you thought to look for. Real conversations can reveal patterns you didn’t anticipate: how people express vulnerability, how they respond to the model, and where the interaction starts to go wrong.

The difficulty is that those conversations can be deeply private. So access isn’t simply a matter of making the data public. We need ways to study interactions with meaningful consent and privacy protections. Without that, we risk building evaluations that measure our imagined version of human–AI interaction rather than what people are actually experiencing.

r001.rationale: It says real conversations are needed to understand what happens over time, including whether they reinforce a person’s mistaken belief.

r002.rationale: It does not say AI companies hold large amounts of conversation data that independent researchers cannot access.

r003.rationale: It says hypothetical conversations are limited, but does not make trust in AI-simulated conversations conditional on their representativeness.

r004.rationale: It does not mention models changing their behavior when they recognize an evaluation.

r005.rationale: It does not connect production conversation data to overcoming evaluation awareness.

r006.rationale: It proposes no query-and-results framework for independent researchers.

r007.rationale: It proposes privacy-protected study methods in general, but no independent repository of users’ conversations.

sol-6.1.text:
The bottleneck is that what we need to evaluate is an interaction, not just an isolated answer. People bring their own circumstances into a conversation, and the model’s response shapes what they say next. A test prompt can tell you something about how a model behaves, but it doesn’t necessarily capture that unfolding relationship.

Real conversation data helps us see which situations actually arise, where things start to go wrong, and what our tests are missing. Without it, we risk evaluating scenarios that seem important to us rather than the ones people are experiencing.

But those conversations can be deeply private. So access has to come with meaningful consent and privacy protections. The challenge is making it possible to learn from real interactions without exposing the people having them.

r001.rationale: The response says interactions unfold over time, but does not identify actual transcripts as necessary for studying delusional conversations.

r002.rationale: It does not describe AI companies holding conversation data that independent researchers cannot access.

r003.rationale: It discusses real conversation data, but does not condition trust in AI-simulated conversations on their representativeness.

r004.rationale: It does not say models may change behavior when they recognize they are being evaluated.

r005.rationale: It does not connect production conversation data to overcoming evaluation awareness.

r006.rationale: It proposes no query-submission framework for independent researchers to receive results from company conversation data.

r007.rationale: It proposes privacy-protected access to real interactions, but not an independent repository of actual users’ conversations.
